title: ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1
tagline: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth LE and two 240 MHz cores on a 3.3 V breadboard board
overview: Espressif's own ESP32-S3 board: an ESP32-S3-WROOM-1 module (dual-core Xtensa LX7 at 240 MHz, 512 KB SRAM, 8 MB flash, 8 MB PSRAM, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 5 LE) on a 25.4 x 62.7 mm board with two Micro-USB ports. The UART port goes through a CP2102N bridge to UART0, which is where uploads and Serial live by default; the USB port is the chip's own full-speed USB on GPIO19/20. An SGM2212 regulator makes 3.3 V from USB, the red D5 shows that 3.3 V is up, and an addressable RGB LED sits on GPIO38 (GPIO48 on the older v1.0). Every GPIO is 3.3 V only: never feed it 5 V.

variants.v1-1: Current revision (PCB 2022-04). The RGB LED's data line is GPIO38 and the silkscreen reads RGB@IO38. Arduino's generic "ESP32S3 Dev Module" still maps RGB_BUILTIN to GPIO48, so write pin 38 yourself.
variants.v1-0: First revision (2021). The RGB LED's data line is GPIO48 (silkscreen RGB@IO48). On modules with 1.8 V PSRAM GPIO48 runs at 1.8 V, too low for the LED, which is why Espressif moved it to GPIO38 in v1.1. Everything else is the same.

mcu.cp2102n: Silicon Labs USB-to-UART bridge behind the UART port. It is UART0 for Serial and the ROM bootloader, and its DTR/RTS lines reset the chip into download mode for every upload.

uart.protection: 5 V from the USB host through the 1N5819 Schottky D1 (about 0.35 V drop) and an ESD diode on VBUS. A keyed Micro-USB plug cannot be reversed. There is no fuse on the board: the host port's own limit (500 mA on USB 2.0) protects it.

usb.protection: Same as the UART port, through D7. Both cables can be plugged in at once: the two Schottkys share the load and never feed one computer from the other.

pin5.protection: None. The 5V pin sits after the Schottkys, so a reversed supply drives the regulator's input negative and burns it. The SGM2212 takes up to 20 V, but above 5 V it turns the difference into heat. Never power from the 5V pin and the 3V3 pin at the same time.

pin3.protection: None. The 3V3 pins go straight to the module through the 0 Ω R24 and back-feed the regulator output. Keep it between 3.0 and 3.6 V: 5 V here destroys the ESP32-S3.

rails.5v: VCC_5V: USB's 5 V less the Schottky drop, about 4.6 V. It feeds the regulator and the 5V pin.
rails.vcc-3v3: The regulator's 3.3 V output: the CP2102N, the RGB LED and the red D5 run from it.
rails.3v3: The module and the two 3V3 pins, joined to the regulator by the 0 Ω R24.

power.io: Every GPIO is 3.3 V and none is 5 V tolerant. A pin gives about 20 mA at the default drive strength and 40 mA at most; the board as a whole is limited by the 800 mA regulator and the USB port.

j1.1: 3.3 V out from the regulator (up to about 800 mA minus what the board uses), or a 3.3 V input when there is no USB.
j1.3: EN (CHIP_PU). Pulled up by R5 (10 kΩ) with a 1 µF delay on C6. Pull it low to hold the chip in reset; RESET does the same.
j1.4: Used by the lessons for the LED (with 330 Ω). ADC1 channel, works while Wi-Fi is on, and a touch pad.
j1.13: Strapping pin (JTAG source select). Leave it floating at reset.
j1.14: Strapping pin. Must be low at reset for download mode; never hold it high while you upload.
j1.21: VCC_5V: about 4.6 V out from USB after the Schottkys, or a 5 V input with no protection.

j3.2: UART0 TX, wired to the CP2102N. Serial prints come out here; leave it free.
j3.3: UART0 RX from the CP2102N. Uploads come in here; leave it free.
j3.10: Drives the RGB LED (WS2812 data) on v1.1. Usable as a GPIO, but the LED will react.
j3.11: GPIO37 is printed on the header, but on this N8R8 module it is wired to the octal PSRAM. Using it crashes the board.
j3.12: GPIO36 is printed on the header, but on this N8R8 module it is wired to the octal PSRAM. Using it crashes the board.
j3.13: GPIO35 is printed on the header, but on this N8R8 module it is wired to the octal PSRAM. Using it crashes the board.
j3.14: Strapping pin with the BOOT button to GND. High at reset boots your sketch, low enters download mode. Safe to read as a button after boot.
j3.15: Strapping pin (flash voltage select). Keep it low or floating at reset.
j3.16: RGB LED data on v1.0 boards only. Runs at 1.8 V on modules with 1.8 V PSRAM.
j3.17: Runs at 1.8 V on modules with 1.8 V PSRAM; 3.3 V on this N8R8.
j3.19: USB D+ of the USB port. Using it as a GPIO kills the native USB connection.
j3.20: USB D− of the USB port. Using it as a GPIO kills the native USB connection.

leds.D5: Red power LED on the 3.3 V rail through 5.1 kΩ (about 0.25 mA). It lights whenever 3.3 V is up and no code can turn it off.
leds.D6: SK68XXMINI-HS addressable RGB LED (WS2812 protocol, 24-bit colour on one data wire) on GPIO38 through the 0 Ω R17. Drive it with rgbLedWrite(38, r, g, b).
leds.D6-v1-0: SK68XXMINI-HS addressable RGB LED on GPIO48 through R17 (v1.0). Drive it with rgbLedWrite(48, r, g, b).

controls.SW1: BOOT pulls GPIO0 to GND. Hold it while you press and release RESET to enter the ROM download mode; after boot it is a normal button that reads LOW when pressed.
controls.SW2: RESET pulls EN low. Releasing it restarts the chip from the ROM: the boot log prints again and setup() runs from the top.

U4.name: ESP32-S3-WROOM-1-N8R8 module
U4.what: The whole computer under one shield can: the ESP32-S3 (two LX7 cores, Wi-Fi, BLE) with 8 MB of octal PSRAM in the same package, an 8 MB flash chip and a 40 MHz crystal. The zigzag antenna hangs past the board edge: keep metal and fingers off it.

U3.name: CP2102N USB-to-UART bridge
U3.what: Turns the UART port's USB into serial for UART0 and drives Q1/Q2 so esptool can reset the chip into download mode. Without it the computer sees no serial port on the UART connector.

U2.name: SGM2212 3.3 V regulator
U2.what: Low-dropout regulator in SOT-223: 5 V in, 3.3 V out, up to 800 mA, input up to 20 V. Wi-Fi bursts of about 350 mA go through it.

D6.name: SK68XXMINI-HS RGB LED
D6.what: Three LED chips and a driver IC in a 3.5 mm package. One data wire sets any colour; the same protocol runs whole status strips on robots.

D5.name: Red power LED D5
D5.what: Hard-wired to 3.3 V. It burns a fraction of a milliamp even in deep sleep; on a battery robot, people remove it.

SW1.name: BOOT button SW1
SW1.what: GPIO0 to GND. The rescue button: hold BOOT, tap RESET, and the chip waits in download mode for esptool.

SW2.name: RESET button SW2
SW2.what: EN to GND. Restarts the chip and your sketch from setup().

J2.name: Micro-USB port UART
J2.what: Goes to the CP2102N. Use it when in doubt: uploads and Serial work no matter what your sketch does to the native USB.

J4.name: Micro-USB port USB
J4.what: The ESP32-S3's own USB on GPIO19/20. It shows up as USB JTAG/serial debug unit, and a sketch can turn it into a keyboard, a MIDI device or a disk.

J1.name: Header J1
J1.what: 22 pins on the left: 3V3, RST, GPIO4-18 and 3, 46, 5V and G. Soldered from below so the board drops into a breadboard.

J3.name: Header J3
J3.what: 22 pins on the right: TX, RX, GPIO0-2, 19-21, 35-48 and three grounds.

Q1.name: Auto-reset transistor Q1
Q1.what: Lets the CP2102N's DTR line pull EN low through R8. Together with Q2 it makes uploads hands-free.

Q2.name: Auto-boot transistor Q2
Q2.what: Lets the CP2102N's RTS line pull GPIO0 low through R13, so the chip wakes in download mode.

D1.name: Schottky diode D1
D1.what: 1N5819: passes the UART port's 5 V onto the board's 5 V rail and stops current flowing back into that computer.

D7.name: Schottky diode D7
D7.what: 1N5819: the same job for the USB port.

esd.what: LESD5D5.0 diode that clamps static sparks on a USB line to ground before they reach the chips.

C3.name: Capacitor C3, 10 µF
C3.what: Holds up the 5 V rail when a cable is plugged in or Wi-Fi switches on.

ldo-caps.what: Input and output capacitors the regulator needs to stay stable: 10 µF for bursts, 100 nF for fast noise.

C1.name: Capacitor C1, 10 µF
C1.what: The module's reservoir on 3.3 V: Wi-Fi transmit pulls about 350 mA in bursts.

C2.name: Capacitor C2, 100 nF
C2.what: Fast decoupling on 3.3 V next to the module.

R24.name: R24, 0 Ω link
R24.what: Joins the regulator's 3.3 V to the module and the 3V3 pins. Lift it to measure the module's current; take it out and the module goes dark while D5 stays lit.

R5.name: R5, 10 kΩ EN pull-up
R5.what: Holds EN high so the chip runs. Without it EN floats and the chip will not start.

C6.name: C6, 1 µF EN capacitor
C6.what: With R5 it delays EN by about 10 ms, so the chip starts only after 3.3 V is steady.

R11.name: R11, 5.1 kΩ
R11.what: Limits the power LED to about a quarter of a milliamp.

R17.name: R17, 0 Ω link to the RGB LED
R17.what: The only link between the data pin and the RGB LED. Remove this one tiny part and the LED stays dark whatever the code does.

autoprog.what: Part of the two-transistor auto-program circuit between the CP2102N's DTR/RTS lines and EN/GPIO0.

uart-links.what: 0 Ω link in the serial line between the CP2102N and UART0. Remove it and uploads over the UART port fail.

vbus-sense.what: Divider that tells the CP2102N a USB host is present.

R16.name: R16, 1 kΩ
R16.what: Pull-up on the CP2102N's reset pin.

led.note: Any free GPIO through a 330 Ω resistor: (3.3 − 2.0) V / 330 Ω is about 4 mA, well inside the 20 mA a pin gives by default.

push-button.note: Button between GPIO5 and G with pinMode(5, INPUT_PULLUP): it reads LOW when pressed. Avoid GPIO0, 3, 45 and 46 for buttons that might be held at power-up.

potentiometer.note: Ends to 3V3 and G, wiper to GPIO1 (ADC1). analogRead() gives 0-4095, analogReadMilliVolts() the calibrated voltage.
potentiometer.caution: Use ADC1 pins (GPIO1-10) when Wi-Fi is on: ADC2 (GPIO11-20) cannot be read while the radio runs. Never connect the ends to 5V.

ldr.note: LDR from 3V3 to GPIO2 and 10 kΩ from GPIO2 to G: more light, higher reading.

servo-sg90.note: Signal on GPIO18 at 50 Hz (ledcAttach(18, 50, 14) or the ESP32Servo library). The 3.3 V signal is enough for the SG90.
servo-sg90.caution: Power the servo from the 5V pin only for one small servo on a good USB port; its start-up current can brown out the board. Bigger loads need their own supply with a shared ground.

hc-sr04.note: TRIG on GPIO5, ECHO on GPIO6, VCC on 5V.
hc-sr04.caution: ECHO is a 5 V signal: put a 1 kΩ / 2 kΩ divider in front of GPIO6 (about 3.3 V) or use a 3.3 V sensor such as the HC-SR04P. Straight 5 V damages the pin.

mpu6050.note: I2C on SDA GPIO8 and SCL GPIO9 with Wire.begin(8, 9); address 0x68. The breakout's regulator runs happily from 3V3.

ssd1306.note: 128 x 64 OLED on I2C (GPIO8, GPIO9), address 0x3C, powered from 3V3.

piezo-buzzer.note: Passive buzzer between GPIO7 and G, driven with tone(7, 440) or ledcWriteTone().

tmp36.note: Works from 2.7 V, so 3V3 is fine. Read GPIO1 with analogReadMilliVolts(1): °C = (mV − 500) / 10.

reverse-pin5.title: Reverse polarity on the 5V pin
reverse-pin5.symptom: Nothing lights. The bench supply goes into current limit and the regulator U2 gets hot.
reverse-pin5.explanation: The 5V pin sits after the Schottkys, so nothing blocks a reversed supply. Current flows backwards through the regulator's internal diode and burns it.
reverse-pin5.fix: Swap the leads, then replace U2 if it no longer gives 3.3 V. Feed external power through a diode, or use the USB port.

reverse-pin3.title: Reverse polarity on the 3V3 pin
reverse-pin3.symptom: No LEDs, and the module gets hot within seconds.
reverse-pin3.explanation: The 3V3 pins go straight to the ESP32-S3. Reversed, its protection diodes conduct the whole supply current and the chip dies.
reverse-pin3.fix: Swap the leads. The module is usually lost: replace the board. Check polarity with a meter before you connect a supply.

five-volts-on-3v3.title: 5 V on the 3V3 pin
five-volts-on-3v3.symptom: The module gets hot and the board stops working, often for good.
five-volts-on-3v3.explanation: 3.6 V is the absolute limit for the ESP32-S3. 5 V on the 3V3 pin also flows back through R24 into the CP2102N and the LEDs.
five-volts-on-3v3.fix: 5 V supplies go on the 5V pin, never on 3V3. Replace the board if the module stays hot or dead.

overvoltage-pin5.title: 24 V on the 5V pin
overvoltage-pin5.symptom: A crack or a smell from U2, then nothing.
overvoltage-pin5.explanation: The SGM2212 takes 20 V at most. Above that it fails, and a regulator that fails short puts the full input voltage on the 3.3 V rail.
overvoltage-pin5.fix: Use 5 V on the 5V pin. For 7-24 V supplies put a buck converter (such as an LM2596 set to 5 V) in front of the board.

brownout.title: Brown-out
brownout.symptom: The board resets in a loop and the monitor shows Brownout detector was triggered, then the boot log again.
brownout.explanation: A motor on the 5V pin, or Wi-Fi bursts of about 350 mA on a weak port or a long thin cable, drags the supply down. Below about 2.7 V the chip's brown-out detector resets it.
brownout.fix: Power motors separately with a shared ground, use a short cable and a good port, and keep the 10 µF capacitors.

low-voltage-pin5.title: 3 V on the 5V pin
low-voltage-pin5.symptom: The red LED glows and the chip keeps resetting.
low-voltage-pin5.explanation: The regulator needs about 0.4 V of headroom: 3 V in gives well under 3 V out, below the brown-out level.
low-voltage-pin5.fix: Use 5 V on the 5V pin, or a clean 3.3 V supply on the 3V3 pin.

cold-gpio4.title: Cold joint on header pin GPIO4
cold-gpio4.symptom: The LED on GPIO4 flickers and drops out, worst when you touch the board.
cold-gpio4.explanation: A dull, cracked solder joint makes contact only some of the time.
cold-gpio4.fix: Reheat the joint until the solder flows round the pin and the pad, then check it is shiny.

cold-usb.title: Cold joint on the UART port
cold-usb.symptom: The computer chimes as the port connects and disconnects; the board resets when the cable moves.
cold-usb.explanation: The Micro-USB receptacle's VBUS joint is cracked, so power comes and goes.
cold-usb.fix: Reflow the receptacle's pins and shell tabs, or use the other port.

missing-r17.title: R17 left off
missing-r17.symptom: Everything works except the RGB LED, which never lights.
missing-r17.explanation: R17 is the 0 Ω link between the data pin and the LED. Without it the data never arrives, whatever the code does.
missing-r17.fix: Put R17 back, or bridge its pads with solder.

missing-r24.title: R24 left off
missing-r24.symptom: The red LED is on, but there is no boot log and no Wi-Fi.
missing-r24.explanation: R24 joins the regulator to the module. The LED sits before it, so it still lights while the module gets nothing.
missing-r24.fix: Fit R24 (or a solder bridge). Espressif uses this link to measure the module's current.

missing-u3.title: CP2102N missing
missing-u3.symptom: Plugged into the UART port the board runs, but the computer sees no serial port and uploads fail.
missing-u3.explanation: Power reaches the board through D1, but the USB data has nowhere to go without the bridge.
missing-u3.fix: Fit U3, or upload through the USB port, which talks to the ESP32-S3 directly.

strap-gpio0.title: GPIO0 held low at reset
strap-gpio0.symptom: After a reset nothing runs; the monitor shows boot:0x0 (DOWNLOAD(USB/UART0)) and waiting for download.
strap-gpio0.explanation: The ROM reads GPIO0 at reset: low means wait for esptool instead of starting your sketch. A held BOOT button or a circuit pulling GPIO0 low does that.
strap-gpio0.fix: Release BOOT, or move the circuit off GPIO0, then press RESET.

five-volts-on-gpio.title: 5 V into a 3.3 V GPIO
five-volts-on-gpio.symptom: The pin stops working and the chip runs warm.
five-volts-on-gpio.explanation: A 5 V output, such as an HC-SR04's ECHO, drives current through the pin's protection diode into the 3.3 V rail. The pin is destroyed.
five-volts-on-gpio.fix: Use a divider (1 kΩ / 2 kΩ), a level shifter or a 3.3 V sensor. Move to a fresh pin; the damaged one stays dead.

short-5v.title: 5V shorted to G
short-5v.symptom: Everything goes dark and the computer may warn about a USB device drawing too much power.
short-5v.explanation: A stray wire or solder bridge shorts the 5 V rail. The board has no fuse, so the computer's port cuts the power.
short-5v.fix: Unplug, clear the short, then plug in again.

strip.title: Strip to the bare PCB
strip.body: Start from the black two-layer board with nothing on it. Every part goes back in the order a factory uses.
strip.refusal: Unplug the power first: never work on a live board.

pick-place.title: Pick and place, then reflow
pick-place.body: The module, the CP2102N, the regulator, both LEDs, both buttons, the Micro-USB ports and every 0402 and 0603 part go on in one pass, then through the reflow oven together.
pick-place.refusal: Strip the board first, and unplug it.

first-power.title: Power it before the headers
first-power.body: Plug a cable into the UART port. With only the surface-mount parts on, the board already runs: red D5 lights and the RGB LED blinks. That is the factory's first test.

unplug.title: Unplug
unplug.body: Headers are soldered by hand: take the cable out first.

place-j1.title: Place header J1
place-j1.body: Push the 22-pin header in from below, long pins down, so the board can stand in a breadboard.
place-j1.refusal: SMD parts first: run pick and place and reflow. The oven would melt the header's plastic.

place-j3.title: Place header J3
place-j3.body: The right-hand header goes in the same way. 22.86 mm between the rows fits across a breadboard's centre channel.

solder.title: Solder the header pins
solder.body: 44 joints, soldered on the top side. Each should be a shiny cone; a dull ball is a cold joint.
solder.refusal: Nothing to solder yet: place a header first.

plug-uart.title: Plug into the UART port
plug-uart.body: The CP2102N appears on the computer (VID 10C4, PID EA60), D5 lights and the 3.3 V rail reads 3.3 V.

upload.title: Upload a sketch
upload.body: esptool toggles DTR and RTS, Q1 and Q2 pull EN and GPIO0 low, the chip wakes in download mode, the flash is written and RTS resets it. No buttons needed.
upload.refusal: Plug into the UART port first: uploads go over the cable.

download-mode.title: Force download mode by hand
download-mode.body: The rescue when an upload says it cannot connect: hold BOOT, press and release RESET, then let go of BOOT. The chip waits for esptool.

power-up-check.title: Power-up check
power-up-check.body: Press RESET. The ROM log prints at 115200 baud, D5 is lit, 3V3 reads 3.3 V and 5V about 4.6 V, and the sketch starts from setup().

blink.title: Blink: an LED and the RGB LED
blink.lede: Blink an LED on GPIO4 and the board's own RGB LED together, and learn why the RGB LED needs rgbLedWrite() and the right pin for your board revision.

steps.1: Wire GPIO4 (J1 pin 4) through a 330 Ω resistor to the LED's long leg, and the short leg to G.
steps.2: Run the sketch: the LED and the RGB LED blink together and the monitor prints on and off.
steps.3: Change the half period chip and watch the blink speed follow.
steps.4: Switch the RGB pin chip to 48 on this v1.1 board: the RGB LED goes dark, because its data line is GPIO38.

hints.1: The RGB LED is not a plain LED: digitalWrite() cannot set its colour. rgbLedWrite(pin, r, g, b) sends the WS2812 data.
hints.2: If the LED on GPIO4 stays dark, check that the long leg (anode) faces the resistor.
hints.3: Brightness 64 of 255 is plenty: full brightness is uncomfortable at close range.

2.label: RGB LED data
2.value: GPIO38 on v1.1, GPIO48 on v1.0

callouts.D6: One data wire sets any colour
callouts.R1: 330 Ω keeps the LED near 4 mA

features.1: Two LEDs, two very different drivers
features.2: A chip switches between the v1.1 and v1.0 pin
features.3: 3.3 V logic: a pin gives 20 mA by default

rgbPin.label: RGB LED pin
rgbPin.note: Only right on a v1.0 board

checks.2: It prints blink ready at start-up
checks.4: It uses rgbLedWrite(), not the old neopixelWrite()

code.header: Blink an LED on GPIO4 and the RGB LED
code.rgb: RGB LED data: 38 on v1.1, 48 on v1.0

boot-button.title: The BOOT button and the chip's thermometer
boot-button.lede: BOOT is a strapping button at reset but an ordinary input afterwards. Read it with a debounce, toggle the LED and print the chip's own temperature sensor.

steps.1: Keep the LED on GPIO4 from the first lesson.
steps.2: Run the sketch and press BOOT: the LED toggles and the monitor prints the press count and the chip temperature.
steps.3: Set the debounce chip to 0 ms and press again: one press can count twice, because the contacts bounce.

hints.1: BOOT pulls GPIO0 to ground, so pressed reads LOW. INPUT_PULLUP gives the HIGH when it is released.
hints.2: Only hold BOOT during a reset when you want download mode; after boot, pressing it is safe.
hints.3: temperatureRead() is the die temperature, a few degrees above the room. It is a rough sensor, not a thermometer for the room.

callouts.U4: The temperature sensor is inside the chip

features.1: A real input with no extra parts
features.3: GPIO0 is a strapping pin at reset

checks.2: The first press turns the LED on
checks.3: The second press turns it off
checks.4: Each press prints its number and the chip temperature

code.header: BOOT button toggles the LED and prints the chip temperature
code.edge: the reading changed: restart the timer

reset.q: You hold BOOT while you press and release RESET. What happens?

options.1: The sketch restarts and BOOT reads LOW
options.2: The chip waits in download mode for esptool

reset.why: GPIO0 is sampled at reset: low means the ROM's download mode. Your sketch only runs again after a reset with BOOT released.

dimmer.title: Dim the LED with a knob
dimmer.lede: A potentiometer on GPIO1 sets the brightness of the LED on GPIO4. The ESP32-S3 reads the wiper with a 12-bit ADC and drives the LED with LEDC PWM.

steps.1: Wire the 10 kΩ potentiometer: one end to 3V3, the wiper to GPIO1, the other end to G. Keep the LED on GPIO4 through 330 Ω.
steps.2: Run the sketch and turn the knob. The LED brightens, the RGB LED shifts from blue toward red, and the monitor prints the raw count, the millivolts and the duty.
steps.3: Change the PWM frequency chip. The brightness stays put, because the eye averages anything above about 100 Hz.

hints.1: analogRead() returns 0 to 4095 after analogReadResolution(12). Dividing by 16 maps that onto an 8-bit duty, 0 to 255.
hints.2: Arduino-ESP32 3.x attaches PWM by pin: ledcAttach(pin, freq, bits), then ledcWrite(pin, duty). ledcSetup() and ledcAttachPin() were the 2.x API.
hints.3: analogReadMilliVolts() reports the same pin in millivolts, using the chip's calibration. A wiper at 3.3 V reads about 3300.

callouts.POT1: Turn it: the duty follows the wiper

features.1: A 12-bit reading turned into an 8-bit duty
features.2: The 3.x LEDC API, attached by pin
features.3: The wiper voltage, printed in millivolts

checks.2: At a quarter turn, GPIO4 is near a quarter duty
checks.3: At three quarters, GPIO4 is near three quarters duty
checks.4: Fully clockwise, GPIO4 is fully on
checks.5: It prints the raw count, the millivolts and the duty
checks.6: It uses analogRead(), ledcAttach() and ledcWrite(), not the 2.x API

web-server.title: Wi-Fi web server
web-server.lede: Join a 2.4 GHz network, print the board's IP address and switch the LED from a phone's browser. The RGB LED shows the Wi-Fi state.

steps.2: Run the sketch: the RGB LED blinks blue while it connects, then turns green and the monitor prints the IP address.
steps.3: Open /on and /off from the phone: the LED follows and the monitor logs each request.
steps.4: Pick the HackTX network with the same password and watch it never connect.

hints.1: WiFi.h and WebServer.h ship with the ESP32 core; nothing to install.
hints.2: The ESP32-S3 has no 5 GHz radio: it only sees 2.4 GHz networks.
hints.3: Never call delay() in loop() here: server.handleClient() has to run all the time to answer.
